papers.title: Seeing new 'stuff' for the very first time
papers.abstract: Humans are excellent at recognizing materials like food, soil or paper, which is crucial for many everyday tasks. We generally enjoy vivid intuitions about what surfaces would feel like, without reaching out and touching them. While this capability is understandable for familiar materials, how does the brain interpret stuff we have never encountered before? We hypothesized that the need to distinguish useful or hazardous substances by sight led to the ability to infer material properties from the very first encounter. To test this, we used generative AI to synthesize realistic images of new 'hybrid' materials, by fusing characteristics of images from different 'parent' categories (e.g., bark x carpet). Even though the hybrid materials have never existed in the real world--and observers judged them to be far less familiar than their parents--we found that they elicited a rich and compelling phenomenology, and yielded consistent inferences about their likely physical and multisensory properties, such as what they would feel like to touch. Their perceived properties occupied the same broad multidimensional space as familiar materials, whereas phase-scrambled controls did not. Our findings suggest that the visual system exploits generalizable relationships between visual appearance and physical properties, enabling instantaneous interpretation of new kinds of 'stuff'.

papers.title: ceTDP: A Practical Tutorial on Valid and Quantitative Cluster-Extent Inference in Neuroimaging
papers.abstract: We introduce ceTDP, a two-stage framework for cluster-extent inference in neuroimaging that extends conventional random field theory-based and permutation-based methods. In contrast to standard cluster inference, which yields binary significance, ceTDP additionally quantifies the proportion of truly active voxels within clusters using the true discovery proportion (TDP). The method is built on closed testing and provides strong family-wise error rate control while remaining consistent with standard cluster inference. The framework operates in two stages: estimation of a cluster-extent threshold, followed by computation of the TDP lower bound. Two complementary procedures are provided: a conservative, statistically guaranteed TDP lower bound (ceTDP-cons) and a heuristic approach for obtaining a potentially tighter estimate of the TDP lower bound (ceTDP-heur). Together, they enable both rigorous inference and improved sensitivity in cluster-level analysis.

papers.title: Self-generated action shapes theta phase alignment at encoding and later recollection
papers.abstract: Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses. These findings link self-generated action to the timing of encoding-related oscillations and to subsequent recollection. The association between later posterior theta alignment and Remember-Know discrimination is consistent with a role for theta phase coordination in associative binding.

papers.title: The emergence and neural organisation of facial-expression information during ultra-brief vision
papers.abstract: A glimpse lasting only a few milliseconds can convey meaningful information about a face, but how the brain transforms such minimal input into stable representations of facial expression and conscious experience remains unclear. Across two experiments using ultra-brief face presentations, we combined hierarchical psychophysical modelling, multivariate EEG decoding, and information-theoretic measures to characterise this transformation. Extending previously reported findings, hierarchical modelling quantified distinct exposure-dependent trajectories for intact-face localisation and expression identification, providing a behavioural calibration of weak, intermediate, and stronger perceptual evidence. The critical neural transition occurred between 4.4 and 6.2 ms. At 4.4 ms, expression sensitivity was behaviourally detectable, but neural expression patterns did not reliably generalise to faces excluded from classifier training. At 6.2 ms, previously observed emotion-related ERP differences were accompanied by expression representations that generalised across faces and locally detectable emotion information during the early posterior negativity (EPN) interval. Subjective clarity tracked location-related neural evidence more consistently than expression-specific evidence, indicating that awareness did not simply mirror the emerging expression representation. The degree to which early centroparietal activity statistically predicted later occipital activity differed between emotional and neutral faces as exposure increased, indicating that the relationship between successive neural responses was reorganised. Thus, a few additional milliseconds of visual input did not merely strengthen facial-expression processing; they transformed weak evidence that did not reliably generalise across faces into more stable, generalisable, behaviourally relevant, and distributed neural information.

papers.title: Prioritization over certainty: Action planning in visual working memory iscoupled with selective attention, rather than action predictability
papers.abstract: When visual information is no longer perceptually available, working memory (WM) allows us to act on sensory representations. But does this guidance require attentional prioritization? We addressed this question by asking participants to remember two oriented bars that were later tested with one predictable and one random probe. This design allowed us to track when a remembered orientation became linked to a specific response hand and whether that link depended on which item was currently prioritized in WM. Response preparation followed prioritization: even when the later response was predictable, no motor preparation emerged while the corresponding item remained latent. Our exploratory analyses showed that prospective action information reduced the need to reprioritize latent items, and that learned stimulus-response mappings generalized across task contexts, suggesting that task-relevant features of visual WM can be partly offloaded onto motor codes. These findings show that active response preparation is coupled with selective attention, while motor representations can also support maintenance in a visual WM task.

papers.title: GESTATIONAL PROTEIN RESTRICTION PROGRAMS SEXUALLY DIVERGENT BEHAVIORAL AGING IN MICE: EARLY AFFECTIVE VULNERABILITY IN MALES AND LATE-LIFE MNEMONIC PRESERVATION AT A HEDONIC COST IN FEMALES
papers.abstract: Maternal protein restriction is a well-established model of developmental programming, yet its consequences for behavior and cognition across the second half of life, and how these differ between sexes, remain poorly characterized. We fed C57BL/6J dams a normal-protein (NP, 17%) or low-protein (LP, 6%) diet throughout gestation and followed male and female offspring with an integrated battery assessing reward sensitivity, locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, social behavior, recognition memory, spatial learning and cognitive flexibility at 12 (middle age) and 18 months (old age). Maternal care was quantified from postnatal days 2 to 9. LP offspring of both sexes were born lighter and caught up by postnatal day 7. LP dams spent more time self-grooming, with longer self-grooming bouts, and took longer to retrieve their pups, whereas licking/grooming, its fragmentation and nursing were unchanged. Middle-aged LP males showed anhedonia-like behavior, anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze, reduced exploration and impaired short-term object recognition; in old age, affective indices normalized, but males became hyperactive and used less efficient search strategies in the Barnes maze. Middle-aged LP females showed hyperactivity, stereotypy and thigmotaxis; at 18 months they developed anhedonia-like behavior yet retained long-term object, social and spatial memory that had declined in aged NP females. A qualitative comparison with a prenatal-stress cohort tested in the same laboratory with the same battery revealed an overlapping, sex- and age-specific signature, particularly for the timing of anhedonia and for late-life memory outcomes. Gestational protein restriction, therefore, programs domain-specific and sexually divergent behavioral aging trajectories rather than uniform cognitive decline. These findings support sex-stratified, life-course designs in fetal programming research.

papers.title: A tuned topographic map hierarchy formats visual working memory load
papers.abstract: Visual working memory tasks rely on neural systems that scale activity with task load. Traditional models assume higher demands are met by monotonically increasing activity within a single process, implying high informational redundancy across responses. However, theories of cognitive control suggest processing strategies change with task demands, flexibly linking sensory inputs to behavior. Using 7T fMRI and neural encoding models, we hypothesized and confirmed that association cortices format task load-dependent responses using sensory-like neural tuning. We identified populations selectively tuned to specific loads, forming 11 topographic maps per hemisphere hierarchically organized from posterior sensory to anterior executive regions across a fronto-parieto-occipital network. Tuning persisted across performance and trial-order controls, was absent without memory task demands, and predicted behavioral accuracy after load changes. These findings demonstrate that human association cortices distribute task demands using continuously varying processing pathways, adapting sensory-like tuning to decorrelate responses and reduce information redundency during cognitive control.

papers.title: Active exploration generates observer-specific image cues for material identity
papers.abstract: When observers interact with an object, each observer generates a different sequence of images. However, which image statistics underlie their perceptual judgments, and whether this self-generated visual input explains what they perceive, remain unclear. We analyzed the first-person recordings of a virtual-reality experiment in which 19 observers judged whether an object was metal or glass while exploring the object with the hand, with the head, with both, and without moving. The object was rendered in two shapes at five levels of physical metallicity and in four illumination environments; every observer saw every stimulus but did so through a different video. Simple image statistics pertaining to the object, to its relation with its surround and to the changes in these properties as the observer explored predicted observers' responses effectively. Critically, when observers disagreed with regard to the same stimulus, their own videos predicted which observer said metal more accurately than chance, and this observer-specific information emerged mainly in the few seconds that preceded the response. The predictive cues identified in this context included the coverage of the optic flow, contrast, highlight coverage, luminance, and the object's luminance and color relative to its surround; furthermore, their importance varied across observers. Thus, active exploration generates different visual evidence for different observers, and their material judgments follow the evidence that they generate.

papers.title: Connectomic Flow Across Cortical Sensory Systems in Juvenile Fibromyalgia
papers.abstract: Adult fibromyalgia (FM) is characterized by altered functional connectivity between sensory, salience, and default mode networks (DMN), yet its early emergence and hierarchical organization remain unclear in Juvenile Fibromyalgia (JFM). We used stepwise functional connectivity (SFC) to detect early changes in the hierarchical integration of sensory signals toward salience and heteromodal networks in adolescents with JFM. Additionally, we assessed whether these alterations overlap with FM-associated gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Forty-six adolescent females with JFM (16.44-1.11 years) and forty-three healthy females (16.09-1.06 years) completed clinical questionnaires and underwent resting-state fMRI. Whole-brain voxel-wise SFC mapped connectivity patterns from primary sensory regions (visual, somatosensory, auditory) toward the DMN across increasing link-step distances. Regression models examined associations between symptom severity and SFC measures. Spatial overlap between functional findings and FM-associated gene expression profiles was also evaluated. Both groups showed a similar pattern, progressing from primary to secondary sensory regions, then to multimodal integration and salience areas, and finally to heteromodal DMN cortices. Greater symptom severity was associated with reduced second-step connectivity between secondary somatosensory cortices and the right anterior insula/operculum (T=5.11, pFWE<0.05). The neuronal transcription factor MYT1L showed relatively higher expression in AHBA in an overlapping region including the pars opercularis. Large-scale sensory-to-heteromodal functional architecture appears preserved in JFM. However, patients with greater symptom burden show reduced propagation of somatosensory information toward salience-interoceptive regions, suggesting altered multimodal processing. This disruption spatially overlaps with MYT1L expression, pointing towards a developmentally sensitive circuit vulnerability in severe patients.

papers.title: Sleep EEG distinguishes learned from novel auditory cues without predicting memory retention in a targeted memory reactivation study
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation during sleep is thought to build on processes initiated during encoding, but how encoding-related brain activity affects individual memories during sleep is unknown. Using targeted memory reactivation (TMR), we tested whether auditory cues elicit memory-related responses during sleep, whether encoding theta and delta power predict these responses, and whether encoding- and sleep-related measures predict long-term retention. Eighty-one healthy young adults learned sound-associated item-face/place pairs during electroencephalography (EEG). Memory was tested before sleep, 12 hours, and 5 days after encoding. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, a subset of learned sounds and novel control sounds were replayed. Item-level mixed-effects models assessed behavioural and EEG predictors of retention success, and item-level correlations related encoding to cue-induced power during sleep. Pre-sleep memory strength and encoding vividness predicted retention, with the vividness effect depending on encoding theta power. TMR did not improve memory and was associated with poorer retention of initially weak memories. Learned cues elicited stronger delta responses than novel sounds during sleep, yet cue-induced delta, theta, and sigma power did not predict retention. Encoding and sleep EEG power were unrelated and showed distinct scalp topographies. In a large item-level dataset, the sleeping brain distinguished learned from novel cues, but this processing did not translate into durable retention, which was instead determined at encoding. Encoding-related oscillations did not relate to memories preferentially reactivated or strengthened by sleep cueing. These findings caution against treating cue-induced sleep oscillations as markers of successful reactivation or consolidation.

papers.title: Influence of Memory Modulation on Affective States in Methamphetamine Use Disorder
papers.abstract: Background: Negative affect and low positive affect are linked to craving and relapse in methamphetamine use disorder (MUD). Brief positive autobiographical memory recall improves mood in non-clinical samples, but it has not been tested in people in treatment for MUD. We tested whether positive memory recall improves affective state, withdrawal and craving compared with a neutral recall condition. Methods: Adults with past-year MUD in their first year of abstinence were recruited from two residential treatment programs in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Participants were randomized, blinded to condition, to recall personally meaningful positive memories (Positive; n = 37) or emotionally neutral procedural memories (Procedural; n = 36) during a laboratory session. Positive and negative affect (PANAS, the prespecified primary outcomes), withdrawal (AWQ), craving (visual digital scale; Stimulant Craving Questionnaire), and anhedonia (SHAPS) were assessed before and approximately one hour after the recall. Group x Time effects were tested with mixed ANCOVAs adjusted for sex and age, with Holm and false discovery rate correction. Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were estimated for each outcome. Results: Of 80 randomized participants, 73 began the session and were analyzed. The Group x Time interaction was not significant for positive affect (p = .689) or negative affect (p = .399). Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were small and imprecise (positive affect: -0.53 points, 95% CI -2.60 to 1.53; negative affect: 0.54 points, 95% CI -0.90 to 1.99). Across both groups, negative affect, withdrawal, craving and desire to use decreased over the session, while positive affect also declined (all p [≤] .015). No secondary or exploratory outcome differed between conditions. Conclusions: A single positive autobiographical memory recall did not produce a detectable end-of-session difference in affect, withdrawal or craving relative to neutral recall in individuals with MUD. Affective and craving states shifted across the session regardless of memory content. Future work should test repeated or more intensive positive-affect interventions in this population.

papers.title: Latent state selection, not outcome integration, resolves approach-avoidance conflict
papers.abstract: Appropriate action selection under approach-avoidance is crucial for survival and emotional resilience. Tasks designed to measure this conflict typically observe response rates at an intermediate rate. However, whether this reflects a single compromised policy or alternation between opposing strategies is unresolved. We trained rats on a novel three trial operant conflict task and recorded anterior insular cortex (aIC) activity with fiber photometry. Fitting a cross-validated GLM-HMM to trial-by-trial choices identified three discrete latent states: a risk-taking state in which rats responded on most conflict trials, a risk-averse state in which they withheld on most conflict trials, and a perseverative state. Rather than integrating the two possible outcomes in conflict, aIC activity flexibly adjusted according to the active state, such that it resembled reward trials in the risk-taking state and punishment trials in the risk-averse state. We also found that acute alcohol increased punished responses by shifting state occupancy. In a yoked Pavlovian cohort, anticipatory aIC signals were reduced, indicating that this encoding requires instrumental agency. Together, these findings suggest that approach-avoidance conflict is resolved by selection between discrete strategies, and that insular recruitment of this process depends on the capacity to act.

papers.title: Discovery of latent clinical phenotypes through optimal transport of brain dynamics
papers.abstract: The increasing availability of large clinical neuroimaging datasets has enabled the discovery of objective, data-driven clinical phenotypes. However, current approaches typically rely on structural or static functional metrics, thereby overlooking the rich information embedded in brain dynamics. To address this limitation, we developed a computational framework combining a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) with Optimal Transport (OT) theory. By representing individual brain dynamics within a shared latent state space, our approach quantifies how much one subject's state-transition dynamics would need to be modified to match another subject's state occupancy distribution, providing a pairwise measure of inter-individual variability that captures temporal aspects of brain function. We applied this framework to multiple sclerosis (MS), a condition where substantial within-group heterogeneity challenges traditional clinical classification. Analyzing resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 122 patients with relapsing-remitting MS and 97 matched healthy controls, the HMM identified three latent states with distinct connectivity patterns. While patients showed an altered temporal organization of recurrent brain states relative to healthy controls, reflected in selective differences in state occupancy and dwell time, we focused on quantifying heterogeneity specifically within the MS cohort. Clustering patients according to OT-based dissimilarities revealed two subgroups with distinct clinical disability and structural disease burden. Crucially, this stratification was not detectable when applying clustering procedures to static functional connectivity, supporting the added value of dynamical features. Our results establish a general methodological framework for extracting clinically relevant phenotypes from temporal brain dynamics, with potential applications across neurological and psychiatric conditions characterized by phenotypic heterogeneity.

papers.title: Childhood Trauma Severity Compounds Reward Anticipation Disruption in Substance Use Disorders
papers.abstract: Background: Substance use disorders (SUD) are associated with reward circuit disruptions and high rates of trauma. Trauma has been found to reduce propensity to engage frontal, limbic, and striatal regions during reward anticipation. However, the interactive effect of trauma and SUD on anticipatory reward circuitry remains unclear. Methods: To address this critical research gap, treatment-enrolled individuals with at least one SUD (N = 150; 78 female) completed questionnaires assessing childhood trauma and current posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and a monetary incentive delay (MID) task during functional magnetic resonance imaging. The MID task presented participants with cues predicting the delivery of no, small, and large monetary gains and avoidance of equally weighted losses. Linear mixed effects models examined the effect of trauma severity or PTSD on percent signal change for anticipation of monetary gains, extracted from a-priori striatal, prefrontal, and mesolimbic anatomic regions of interest. Results: 70.7% of individuals experienced significant childhood trauma and 63.3% met self-report symptom thresholds for probable PTSD. Current PTSD symptoms were positively associated with emotion dysregulation, emotional impulsivity, and drug craving, but were not related to anticipatory BOLD signal. Higher childhood trauma severity (but not current PTSD severity) was associated with lower anticipatory responses within the nucleus accumbens, caudate, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior insula to both gain and loss cues. Conclusions: Childhood adversity is associated with blunted reward anticipation across striatal, prefrontal, and limbic circuitry. This highlights the importance of considering childhood trauma severity in SUD treatment, which may require targeted interventions beyond standard cognitive behavioral therapy to restore normative salience processing, such as striatal neuromodulation.

papers.title: Jump: Making Large-Scale Connectomics Accessible
papers.abstract: Large-scale connectomic resources generated from volumetric electron microscopy (EM) have transformed neuroscience by enabling detailed 3D reconstructions of cellular and subcellular morphology and connectivity across hundreds of thousands of cells in diverse tissues and organisms. Recent advances in machine learning-based cell classification and automated segmentation have enabled large-scale annotation of these datasets, yet barriers remain in validating automated classifications and extracting biological insights. To address these challenges, we developed Jump, a suite of user-friendly web-based platforms generated using Claude. These platforms support interactive exploration, expert-guided community review, and quantitative analysis of multiple publicly available EM datasets, while building a growing repository of community-generated annotations. Using uJump, which hosts data from the MICrONS mouse visual cortex dataset, as an example, we demonstrate rapid retrieval of specific cell populations, region-of-interest filtering, biological inspection of cells, and extraction of quantitative morphological and spatial metrics. We showcase analytical features including cell abundance and spatial organisation, connectivity, local cellular neighbourhoods, and volumetric measurements. Using pericytes and endothelial cells as a case study on the cortical vasculature, we further demonstrate how manual review and reclassification can generate accurately identified cell populations for downstream analyses. Consistent with the open-science principles underpinning many large-scale EM resources, Jump is designed to enable broad community participation. By lowering technical barriers to the use of EM datasets, Jump increases analytical efficiency and promotes collaborative efforts to accurately classify cells and structures. Expert-reviewed annotations can be shared across the community, allowing users to build on existing work rather than repeatedly validating the same automated classifications. Collectively, Jump will help researchers to accelerate biological discovery from connectomic datasets.

papers.title: Does Denoising Reduce Cross-Vendor Variability in Diffusion MRI? A Travelling Heads Evaluation
papers.abstract: Between-scanner variability in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived features can be comparable to biological between-subject variability, even for the same individual scanned at different sites. MRI harmonisation is therefore an essential tool to ensure studies are generalisable across sites, reducing between-scanner variability and enabling pooling of data to achieve large sample sizes and more representative population samples. Denoising using MPPCA is widely used in preprocessing pipelines for diffusion MRI acquisitions to improve image SNR and it has been proposed as an implicit way of harmonising data. In this registered report, we hypothesised that denoising reduces cross-scanner variability and improves reliability in diffusion MRI metrics without changing cross-scanner bias, and that susceptibility-induced off-resonance reduces its efficacy. We tested these hypotheses using a travelling-heads resource of ten subjects scanned on six scanners from three vendors (GE, Philips, Siemens), with within-scanner repeats. We found that: i) Denoising reduced voxel-wise cross-scanner coefficients of variation for fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) and mean kurtosis (MK) (BF > 100; median -3%, -9% and -32%). ROI-wise, variability decreased for MK (-12%), increased for FA (+8%), and evidence was inconclusive for MD. ii) Contrary to our hypothesis, denoising changed cross-scanner bias in every subject-scanner pair, by up to 3% of the mean; in exploratory analyses, this change was strongly related to contrast-to-noise ratio. iii) Evidence for a change in the registered measure of reliability was inconclusive, although exploratory analyses showed higher voxel-wise reliability after denoising. iv) There was no convincing evidence that off-resonance reduces denoising efficacy. Together, these results suggest that MPPCA denoising reduces the random, noise-driven component of cross-scanner variability, most strongly at the voxel level and for kurtosis, but does not consistently reduce systematic differences between scanners. As such, it should complement harmonisation, not replace it.

papers.title: Sampling the Training Trajectory of Vision Models Reveals a Mismatch with Human Visual Development
papers.abstract: We compare time-resolved EEG representational geometry across seven age groups, from 6 months to adulthood, with representations sampled throughout training from supervised and self-supervised ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16. Previous model-brain comparisons mostly used adult brain recordings and untrained or fully trained networks. We find that successive training stages do not systematically progress from child- to adult-like neural representations: alignment with every age group from 4 years onward emerges early in training and remains stable. Training adds substantial alignment beyond the untrained architecture, similarly at every age. Finally, categorical structure and spatial frequency each explain a stable share of the neural geometry at every age, with apparent age-related increases in categorical organization reflecting increased EEG reliability. Because standard training on full-resolution images aligns with all ages early, and spatial frequency, which depends on maturing visual acuity, strongly shapes the neural geometry, developmentally structured visual input may help models follow human visual development.

papers.title: Benchmarking machine learning across development reveals stage-specific neuroanatomical sex signatures.
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) offers powerful approaches for identifying multivariate patterns in neuroimaging data, yet the biological validity and interpretability of the discriminative patterns learned by such models remain incompletely understood. Here, we benchmarked multiple ML approaches for sex classification across development (8-21 years) on structural neuroimaging data and investigated the effects of age on model performance and feature stability. Linear and nonlinear models demonstrated comparable classification performance, indicating that high predictive accuracy can be achieved without relying on highly complex architectures; however, age-stratified analyses and cross-age generalization tests demonstrated that developmental stage influences classification performance, and consistency of learned neuroanatomical features. To assess biological interpretability, we applied SHAP and LIME explainability methods and developed a comprehensive framework for translating feature attributions into biologically interpretable patterns. Sex-discriminative regions were distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical structures and exhibited marked developmental variation. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of interpretable ML for developmental neuroimaging and highlight the importance of evaluating predictive performance while simultaneously taking biological validity, developmental specificity, and attribution stability into consideration.

papers.title: Joint Representation of Valence and Arousal in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: Scenes varying in emotional content are commonly characterized along two affective dimensions: hedonic valence, reflecting pleasantness, and emotional arousal, reflecting intensity. Although prior studies have examined neural representations of valence and arousal separately, it remains unclear how these dimensions are represented jointly and how their representation relates to low-level visual and scene-level properties. Here, we used representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify brain regions whose activity patterns represented the joint valence-arousal structure of affective images and to compare this representation with those of low-level visual and scene-level properties. Twenty participants viewed 60 International Affective Picture System (IAPS) images during simultaneous EEG-fMRI recording. We constructed three image-level representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs): an Emotion RDM derived from valence and arousal ratings; a GIST RDM derived from low-level visual features captured by GIST descriptors; and a Scene RDM derived from CLIP-ViT image embeddings. Searchlight fMRI RSA identified joint valence-arousal representations in lateral occipitotemporal cortex, low-level visual representations in visual cortex, with smaller extensions into right STS and right insula, and scene-level representations across distributed occipital, temporal, parietal, and frontal regions. The valence-arousal representation showed little spatial overlap with the low-level visual representation but was spatially nested within regions representing scene-level properties. EEG-fMRI fusion further indicated that low-level visual representations emerged at approximately 124 ms after stimulus onset, followed by scene-level and valence-arousal representations at approximately 428 ms and 532 ms, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that joint valence-arousal representations are linked to higher-order scene representations, are distinct from low-level visual representations in both space and time, and may support the affective-semantic characterization of visual scenes. Exploratory analyses further showed that valence and arousal ratings generated by multimodal large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) corresponded closely with human ratings and yielded neural representation maps that substantially overlapped with the human valence-arousal map.

papers.title: A Platform for Semi-automatic Segmentation, CharacteristicShape Analysis and Simulation of Neuronal Nuclei
papers.abstract: Segmenting neuronal somas in 3D brain images obtained through techniques such as tissue clearing and Light Sheet Fluorescence Microscopy promises to advance our understanding of healthy brains and the pathophysiological roots of neurological diseases. However, manual segmentation methods are often costly and time-consuming. Automating the segmentation through deep neural networks shows promise, but requires labeled ground-truth data that is also labor-intensive and expensive to obtain. To address these limitations, this work provides a platform within the open-source 3D image analysis software Vaa3D to efficiently and precisely label and automatically segment neuronal somas. A binary image of segmented somas is generated using a region-growing algorithm applied on 3D somas marked and bounded by a sphere around their center of mass, guided by a local Otsu threshold that can be manually overridden. The platform further supports principal component analysis of the segmented somas, allowing them to be rotated about their center of mass and aligned, in order for their characteristic shape to be captured in a probabilistic model. Finally, the platform supports the simulation of soma segmentation: it probabilistically reorients, repositions, and deforms segmented somas obtained from real data, generating synthetic ground truth data that can be used to train deep neural networks.

papers.title: Mouse pup ultrasonic vocalization repertoires shift with age and behavioral context across the first postnatal week
papers.abstract: Pup ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) are thought to communicate and elicit maternal care, yet the structure of the pup call repertoire and how it changes across the vulnerable first postnatal week remain poorly characterized. Here we analyzed approximately 59,000 USVs emitted by wildtype mouse pups (postnatal days P0-P5) during a pup retrieval paradigm that included habituation, pup isolation, and retrieval phases, performed with wild-type (WT) and Mecp2-heterozygous (Het) female mice as alloparental surrogates. Using DeepSqueak-based acoustic feature extraction and unsupervised clustering, we identified eight distinct call types, grouped into two broad classes based on shared acoustic properties. The relative prevalence and sequencing of these call types shifted systematically with postnatal age and behavioral phase, indicating that the pup vocal repertoire is both developmentally and contextually dynamic during the first postnatal week. However, call-type composition and acoustic characteristics did not differ with behavioral outcome, consistent with the model in which USVs function as general arousal signals integrated with other sensory cues. A candidate sequence-level pattern distinguished failed retrievals but was based on few calls and requires further validation. Pup call repertoire and developmental trajectory were also indistinguishable between WT and Het surrogates, indicating that the previously reported retrieval deficit in Het females does not arise from atypical pup vocal signals. Together, these results provide a detailed developmental and contextual map of the early pup call repertoire and a framework for relating call-type dynamics to auditory circuit plasticity across early postnatal life.

papers.title: The computational cost of explicit strategies in force-field adaptation
papers.abstract: Sensorimotor adaptation is often attributed to an implicit, cerebellar-based process, particularly when learning to compensate for novel limb dynamics. However, recent evidence suggests that explicit strategies can also contribute to force-field adaptation, although how these strategies are represented and implemented is unclear. In visuomotor adaptation, explicit strategies can rely on an algorithmic-like process in which the time required to prepare a movement increases with the magnitude of the required correction. Here, we asked whether explicit compensation for force-field perturbations is generated through a similarly time-consuming computation. Human participants performed reaching movements in a paired-trial paradigm in which the force experienced on one movement could be used to prepare a counteracting response on the subsequent movement. Across two experiments, we found that when participants were encouraged to attempt to counteract the forces, movement preparation time increased systematically with force magnitude: larger compensatory responses required longer preparation. This relationship was substantially reduced when participants performed exactly the same task but were not informed about the paired-trial design, performance was significantly worse and was not accompanied by a corresponding increase in preparation time. These findings suggest that when participants use a strategy to improve performance in response to perturbing forces, it appears to be accomplished with a parametric, algorithmic-like process, one may be similar to strategies employed in visuomotor adaptation.

papers.title: Excitation/Inhibition Balance in People at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: A Functional MRI Study
papers.abstract: Excitation/inhibition (E/I) imbalance is implicated in the pathophysiology of psychosis, but the extent to which this is evident before the onset of illness is unclear. Here, we investigated E/I-related brain dynamics using the Hurst exponent (HE) derived from resting-state MRI in two longitudinal cohorts of individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P): PSYSCAN (190 CHR-P individuals and 115 controls) and Accelerating Medicines Partnership(R) Schizophrenia (826 CHR-P individuals and 241 controls). Both cohorts showed lower whole-brain HE in CHR-P individuals than in controls at baseline, with the most prominent differences observed in the somatomotor network and thalamus. In both cohorts, normative receptor distributions significantly predicted the spatial pattern of HE differences, with consistent contributions from norepinephrine, serotonin, and opioid receptors. In PSYSCAN, 21 CHR-P individuals transitioned to psychosis during follow-up. There was preliminary evidence that subsequent transition to psychosis was associated with a longitudinal reduction in HE in the right inferior parietal cortex and that baseline regional HE showed above-chance prediction of subsequent transition at the individual level. Together, these findings suggest that vulnerability to psychosis is associated with reduced HE, consistent with less persistent brain dynamics and increased excitability.

papers.title: Neuronal communication subspaces arise across prefrontal-striatal circuits prior to gaze-directed object selection and develop with learning
papers.abstract: How neuronal ensembles determine the most relevant object to attend to remains unresolved but likely involves coordinating information across multiple brain areas. We found support for this hypothesis in latent firing co-variations across the prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and head of the caudate (CD) during and after attention-set learning. Before gaze shifted to an object, neuronal communication subspaces emerged across area pairs. While exploring options during learning, ACC and PFC led communication over the CD prior to gaze shifts, which switched to the CD and PFC leading the ACC when exploiting learned attention sets. Neurons participating in exploration- and exploitation-specific subspaces were partly segregated and carried information about the value and location of the to-be-selected objects, suggesting they guide attention and gaze.

papers.title: An Open, Evolving Brain and Cognitive Aging Simulator Enabled by Agentic Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: An agentic AI simulator was built to advance our understanding about how the human brain and cognition change with age. The simulator generates worlds based on hypothesized age-linked cascades and then simulates studies across varied experimental designs and selection criteria. Each simulated world begins with 120,000 individual lives initiated by baseline parameters (e.g., genetic risk, birth year) and then changed by age-dependent cascades (e.g., amyloid-dependent, cardiovascular). Examples illustrate how the simulator predicts distinct data patterns in cross-sectional versus longitudinal designs, how alternative participant selection strategies emphasize baseline differences versus age-related decline, and how variable levels of association emerge between brain and cognition dependent upon design choices. Simulations of clinical trials provide information about design, power, and outcome considerations. Experiments on alternative simulated worlds evaluate how well hypothesized cascades accommodate real-world data patterns, capturing the insights and open puzzles inside the application. Most critically, the application is built to evolve. Its code contains a complete description of how to construct and update itself so that any person or AI agent can explore a new finding, recalibrate to emerging data, or build and simulate a novel future study. The simulator is offered as a tool for understanding data patterns, teaching, and generation of hypotheses to be tested in future studies using real-world data collection.

papers.title: Reciprocal 16p11.2 Copy Number Variants Differentially Alter Regional Brain Anatomy and Allometric Scaling
papers.abstract: Reciprocal 16p11.2 copy-number variants (CNVs) confer substantial risk for neuropsychiatric disorders and produce opposing effects on brain size, with larger brain volume in deletion carriers and smaller volume in duplication carriers. Regional alterations broadly parallel this global phenotype, but because regional brain measures scale nonlinearly with brain size, it remains unclear whether regional differences reflect expected consequences of altered brain size, regional anatomy disproportionate to brain size, or fundamental alterations in allometric scaling. We analyzed 285 imaging sessions from 235 participants (49 deletion, 59 duplications, 127 controls) using log-log allometric models to distinguish these possibilities. Brain-size adjustment revealed widespread cortical disproportion in both CNVs, with predominantly reciprocal effects driven by surface area rather than cortical thickness, whereas subcortical structures showed convergent reductions disproportionate to brain size. Strikingly, examining genotype-specific scaling exponents revealed distinct allometric patterns between the CNVs. In duplication, regional differences predominantly reflected fixed shifts relative to brain size. In deletion, by contrast, regional differences more frequently varied with brain size, with substantial exponent deviations affecting 32% of disproportionate cortical regions compared with 12% in duplication. Thus, reciprocal 16p11.2 dosage does not simply shift regional anatomy in opposite directions: duplication largely preserves the normally conserved scaling of regional anatomy with brain size, whereas deletion more extensively disrupts it.

papers.title: Neurogenic archetypes and diversifiers configure the molecular and functional organization of corticofugal output channels
papers.abstract: Cortical extratelencephalic neurons (ET) derive from either direct neurogenesis from radial glia cells (ETd) or indirect neurogenesis through intermediate progenitors (ETi), but whether and how neurogenic origin contributes to ET diversity and function remains unknown. Using genetic strategies that differentially target ETd and ETi, we profiled their transcriptomes across the isocortex and imaged their activity in motor cortex during a reach-grasp-drink (RGD) task. While both ETd and ETi contribute to all transcriptomically-defined ET subtypes, they diverge significantly in the concerted expression profile of effector-gene families that shape transcriptional regulation, neuronal connectivity and physiology. During the RGD task, motor cortex ETd formed a small yet heterogeneous pool of broadly tuned activity archetypes, while ETi included a diversified set of spatially organized subpopulations that tracked successive actions of RGD. Therefore, neurogenic origin defines a developmental axis of neuronal diversification orthogonal to the current transcriptomic classification scheme, in which ETi differ from ETd transcriptomically through coordinated significant shifts in effector-gene families, while functionally in the motor cortex, they elaborate a small pool of task-generic ETd into specialized output channels that track different phases of goal-directed RGD behavior.

papers.title: Multicellular nodules form at subacute time points following closed-head diffuse traumatic brain injury in pigs
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of long-term neurological impairments and is associated with persistent neuroinflammation. Multicellular nodules, composed of densely aggregated myeloid cells, have been reported in human post-mortem tissue following TBI but remain poorly characterized. Here, we utilized a clinically relevant porcine model of closed-head diffuse TBI generated through rotational acceleration to characterize the temporal and spatial distribution of these nodules. Nodules were rare in sham animals and minimally present at acute time points but increased significantly by 14 days post injury. Nodule burden increased as a function of injury severity and was positively correlated with rotational injury velocity. Nodules were enriched within white matter structures, including subcortical white matter, corpus callosum, fornix, and internal capsule, while remaining minimally present in cortical gray matter. Within these regions, nodules exhibited a widespread yet spatially organized distribution rather than local clustering around a single anatomical location. Together, these findings demonstrate that multicellular nodules are a robust and reproducible neuroinflammatory pathology following diffuse TBI in a gyrencephalic large-animal model. By establishing the temporal progression, severity dependence, and white matter enrichment of this clinically relevant but understudied endophenotype, this work provides a foundation for future investigations into the mechanisms and consequences of post-traumatic neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Methods for precise targeting and modulation of the axon initial segment
papers.abstract: The axon initial segment (AIS) is fundamental to action potential initiation, neuronal polarity maintenance, and plasticity. Despite its functional importance, AIS remains understudied partially due to the lack of molecular tools with high subcellular specificity. By engineering an ultra-high affinity (Kd ~0.37 nM) small binder (16 kDa) that exclusively targets 480-kDa ankyrin-G, the master scaffold of AIS, and integrating neuronal type-specific promoters with feedback-regulated expression elements, we developed an efficient, portable method for delivering tightly controlled amounts of proteins or organelles to the AIS with unprecedented specificity, enabling selective, tunable, and near-endogenous-level AIS targeting in defined neuronal populations both in vitro and in vivo. Coupled with a toolkit of AIS modulators that we characterized, this strategy achieves directed manipulation of AIS structure, real-time monitoring of AIS plasticity dynamics and fast degradation of the entire AIS compartment, in desired neuronal types. Thus, our method provides new opportunities for dissecting AIS physiology and pathology, facilitating the development of therapeutics for AIS-linked brain disorders.

papers.title: Brain pericyte lineages converge on a shared molecular profile
papers.abstract: Brain pericytes arise from two embryonic lineages, neural crest and mesoderm, but it is unknown whether these origins produce molecularly distinct pericyte populations. Using zebrafish lineage-tracing transgenics, we mapped neural crest- and mesoderm-derived pericytes across the brain from larval to adult stages. Neural crest-derived pericytes occupied the forebrain and mesoderm-derived pericytes occupied the midbrain and hindbrain at early stages. A population of neural crest-derived pericytes then appeared in the dorsal midbrain by 10 days post-fertilization and persisted into adulthood. A small population of mesoderm-derived pericytes also appeared in the ventral forebrain of juvenile and adult fish. Bulk RNA sequencing of FACS-isolated adult pericytes showed that the two lineages share expression of canonical pericyte genes, with only 30 genes differentially expressed. Fluorescent in situ hybridization validated one neural crest-enriched gene, plpp3, and several mesoderm-enriched genes, including loxl2b. Together, these data suggest that despite distinct embryonic origins and regional bias, brain pericyte lineages converge on a largely shared molecular profile.
